title: The king and his sons (Kern ch. 25)
hookLine: two princes lead their father to the teaching

cards: Two young princes want to hear a Buddha teach. Their father, the king, follows a different teaching and isn't interested. So the boys go to their mother first, and her advice is unexpected.
Don't sneak off, she says, and don't argue with him. Go to your father and show him something. Let him see, so his mind turns clear.
That's chapter twenty-five of the Lotus Sutra, in Kern's numbering: a family story from a past age that runs backward from the way families usually work.

teach.h: THE SONS WALK ON THE AIR.
teach.b: Here's what the sons do, as the chapter tells it. They rise into the air in front of their father and walk there, sit there, lie down there, as if the sky were a floor. Water and fire stream from their bodies.
They grow vast, then small again. The king is astonished, and glad.
Who is your teacher, he asks. A Buddha, they answer, teaching the Lotus not far from here. Then I want to see him too, says the king.
Notice the direction. Teaching usually flows downhill, from parent to child. Here it runs uphill.
The sons don't lecture their father; they show him, and let him ask.

teach.h: A TURTLE AND A FLOATING LOG.
teach.b: They also ask their parents' leave to become monks, and the chapter gives a picture for how rare it is to meet a Buddha: like a turtle adrift on the ocean, surfacing right into the hole of a floating log.
Then the whole family goes. The king hears the teaching, and in time he leaves his throne to practice. Here's the chapter's heart.

teach.h: MY SONS ARE MY GOOD FRIENDS.
teach.b: The king tells the Buddha that his two sons have been his good friends; they turned him around. The Buddha agrees: a good friend is a great cause, the one who leads another to see a Buddha and set out on the path.
And the ending reveals who these people became.
The two sons are the Medicine King, whose story came a few days ago, and his brother. A good friend, in this sutra, can be your own child.

how: In Mahayana communities that read the Lotus Sutra, this chapter is taught as a story about the good friend, the person who leads another toward the teaching, and it ties back to the Medicine King chapter, since the two princes are revealed to be the Medicine King and his brother.

games.q: you're one of the two princes. you want to hear the Buddha, and your father follows a different teaching. what do you do?
o: go to him and show him something he can see.
games.why: on their mother's advice, the sons go to their father and show him wonders in the air. he's glad, and asks who taught them.

practice: Bring to mind someone younger than you: a child, a niece, a student, the new person at work. Find one thing they know or see better than you do, small or not small at all.
For a minute, let it be true that they could lead you somewhere.

wordCard.voice: The king and his sons. A father led to the teaching by his own children, who showed him instead of arguing. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: a good friend, someone who helps another toward the path.

carryVoice: Your line: the sons led the king. Sometimes the wonder comes first, and the question follows. See you tomorrow.
